changes: Teams: install a Software team into your project from the Agents panel (Add a team): a product owner, tech lead, implementer, reviewer, QA and release manager, each a Markdown file in .sldev/agents you can edit and commit. Files already there are kept. Start a mission as any role in one click, or let a Lead hand work to a role. Evals tagged with a role pick the best agent for it, a Lead's card shows its workers by role, and the Software team recipe runs the roles from spec to pull request description. You still approve the stories and the spec, review the branch and push. The new Teams guide at /docs/teams walks through it.

GitHub Workflows panel: Workflows and Runs start closed, each with its count, so the panel opens as two short headers. An open section is only as tall as its rows, and a long workflow list keeps to 40% of the panel, so the Runs header is never pushed to the bottom. Runs are compact rows again instead of cards, so twice as many fit.

CLI 0.6.5: when a newer sldev is out, the sidebar shows one card with an Update now button. A click on it (or on the ↑ chip in the status bar, or Ctrl-b u) runs npm install -g sldev-cli@latest in a new tab, so you can watch it. Popups on an empty screen no longer sit on top of the welcome card.

CLI 0.6.5: runtimes, the commands you run often in a project. sldev runtime add ls ls -lrt keeps one in .sldev-cli/runtimes.json, and the project's own scripts (package.json, Makefile, justfile, Cargo, go, compose) are listed after it. Ctrl-b r (or Runtime… in New tab) runs one in a new tab, + adds one and x removes one; sldev runtime start <name> does the same from a script. The command is typed into a shell, so the tab is a shell again when it ends, and after a reboot it reopens without running anything.

sldev-io is now free and open source. There is no trial, no license key and no locked screen any more: every feature works for everyone, and the source is on GitHub under Apache-2.0. If it saves you time, star it on GitHub or sponsor it from Settings → About (or Help: Sponsor sldev-io on GitHub in the command palette). The app no longer asks the website for a beta window or a license, so it makes one fewer network request.

Activity charts in GitHub stats: commits per day over the last 7 or 30 days (per week over 90), with merge commits highlighted and who made the most, and pull requests opened against merged. The commit counts are exactly what git log lists for the range; days follow your own time zone. Hover a bar for its numbers. Pull requests need the GitHub CLI; without it that chart says so and the commit chart still shows.

GitHub stats: a panel with your repository at a glance, opened from the chart button in the Git view or Git: GitHub stats in the command palette. Tiles for open pull requests (and the ones for your branch), open issues, the latest release, the last CI runs on your branch with their status, how far your branch is ahead or behind and the last commit; each one opens on GitHub. It reads again every minute while it is on screen and never in the background. Without the GitHub CLI you still get the branch and last commit, with a Set up gh button.

Worktrees in the Git view: every worktree of the repository is listed, the main checkout marked, with its uncommitted files, commits of its own and the mission, factory run or eval working in it. New worktree makes one by hand, on a new branch from any base or on an existing branch, next to the mission worktrees in .sldev-worktrees. Each one opens in a terminal, your editor or the file manager, and Remove asks first: never while something runs in it, uncommitted work only after you tick discard, the branch only if you ask. Worktrees whose folder is gone get a Prune button.

Git in the activity bar: a Git view shows your branch, what it tracks, how far ahead and behind it is and how many files changed, with Fetch and Pull buttons (also in the command palette as Git: Fetch and Git: Pull). Pull only fast-forwards: a branch that has diverged is left alone and git's message says why. The view refreshes when you come back to the window.

Branches in the Git view: your local branches with their last commit time, remote ones folded underneath. Click one to switch to it; with uncommitted changes the switch is refused and nothing changes. New branch asks for a name (with a hint when git wouldn't take it), what to base it on and whether to switch to it. Right-click a branch to copy its name or open a terminal where it is checked out.

sldev skills: plan with your agent in the terminal and the plan lands in sldev-io as a draft. Add the skills from Skills → Add to this project (or sldev skills install, or npx skills add ben42-01/downloads.sldev.io) and any agent can draft a mission with its brief and acceptance criteria, write board stories with their order, or write a factory recipe or an eval. Missions show up under Saved for later with who drafted them, stories in Proposed; nothing starts until you launch or approve it.

Review by purpose, not by file: the Review tab opens on a walkthrough. The change is split into parts in reading order with the ask and its acceptance criteria on top; lockfiles, generated files and whitespace-only hunks are folded, and auth, billing, migrations, new dependencies, removed tests, secrets and new code nothing uses are flagged. Explain the change has an agent say why each part exists, whether it was asked for, a simpler way and what could break, and a bar shows how much of the diff nobody asked for. Mark parts Looks good, Send back with a note or Cut it (A, S, J/K from the keyboard), Ask why about one part, and send every note back to the agent as one follow-up.

Cards that wait for others: a Board card can wait for other cards (Waits for, by number). Pick-up skips it until they are Done, then starts it on its own; the card says what it waits for and what it unblocks, and loops are refused. Story-writing agents set it too, with after.

What the work took: a finished card shows its time from start to finish, how many agents worked on it, and for Claude Code and Codex the tokens and their cost at list prices. The Done column adds them up.
Copy as PR description: a card's story, the agent's report of what changed, the acceptance criteria as boxes to tick, how to check it and Closes #issue, as Markdown for your pull request.

Retros into memory: on a finished card, a read-only agent looks back at what was sent back, failed or corrected in review and saves at most three lessons to .sldev/memory.md, which every later mission reads.
Release notes from Done: the cards finished since the last notes, grouped into New, Fixes, Docs and Under the hood, to edit and copy; mark them released and the next notes start after them.

Share the board through git: keep the cards in .sldev/board.json and commit it. Teammates' changes come in after a pull (the newer side of each card wins, deletions stick), runs stay on the machine that ran them, and conflict markers stop the sync instead of being overwritten. Nothing is committed for you.

Tune your prompts with evals: prompt variants in .sldev/evals/prompts go before an eval's brief, and Run evals compares them side by side for every agent, with a copy button on the leaderboard for the winner.

Lead missions: give one agent a big goal and it becomes the Lead. It plans, delegates the parts to other agents (Claude, Codex or any agent with the sldev tools) running in parallel in their own worktrees, reviews each diff against the acceptance criteria, sends work back with feedback, and merges the good branches into its own with your tests as the check. Agent "auto" picks the agent that scored best on your evals. Workers show inside the Lead's card in Mission Control, limits are hard (6 workers, 3 at once), and nothing is pushed: you review the Lead's branch. A Board card can start with a Lead too.

Evals: measure agents and models on your own code. An eval is a small YAML file in .sldev/evals: a brief, the commit to start from, and checks (a command that must pass, output it must print, a limit on the diff, or a judge agent with a rubric). Mission Control → Evals runs a suite against any agents and models, each attempt in its own worktree, and shows a matrix per eval, a leaderboard by pass rate, partial credit, time and diff size, and a Markdown scoreboard to copy. Save as eval on any mission turns a real task into one. Nothing is pushed.

Write stories with an agent: describe a feature on the Board and an agent reads the code, then splits it into well-defined stories with why, what to change, acceptance criteria and how to check. They land in Proposed with the agent's name on them; approve them one by one or all at once and they become Agent ready. Refine with an agent rewrites a vague Backlog card in place (and splits it if it's several pieces of work). Nothing is edited while it writes, and agents without the sldev tools hand their stories back as a file.
The Board has its own tab, a button on the activity bar that counts stories waiting for your approval, and a Board menu for new cards, stories, GitHub issues, Approve all and pick-up.

Board and GitHub: import open issues as cards (pick which, filter by label, P1 or urgent labels come in as high priority). A card's factory run closes its issue with the pull request, and a merged pull request moves the card to Done.

Agents file follow-up work: with the sldev tools, an agent that finds something it shouldn't fix now (a missing test, a bug next door) adds a card to Proposed with sldev_board_add, and can read the board with sldev_board. A person decides what an agent picks up next.

Board: plan work on the Board (its own button on the left), with columns Backlog, Proposed, Agent ready, In progress, Review and Done, plus labels and priorities. Turn on Auto pick-up and the factory takes Agent ready cards itself (highest priority first, as many at once as you choose), as a factory run or a mission. Each card follows its run to Review, and a question or a failure shows on the card. Drag cards between columns; nothing is pushed without your click.

Recap: Mission Control → Recap writes a standup (since your last working day), today or this week from your missions, as Markdown grouped into done, ready for review, in progress and blocked, with branches, diffs, agent time and a line from each report. Copy it or save it as a note; it is made on your machine and nothing is sent.
Mission Control: cards fit the four narrow columns (the diff sits next to the branch), cards no longer repeat their column's status, and empty columns say what lands there.

Light theme: Settings → Appearance now offers Dark, Light and Match system. Terminals, notes, reviews and the window frame change with it, and status colours keep their meaning in both. Switch from the command palette too (Toggle light / dark theme).
Interface size: make the whole window 90%, 110% or 125% in Settings → Appearance. Terminal text keeps its own font size on top.
Command palette: the letters you typed are marked in each result, the commands you ran last come first, and a footer shows the keys.
Smoother: menus and the palette open with a short fade, buttons respond when pressed, and the window cross-fades when the theme changes. Turn on reduced motion in your OS and all of that stays still.
Open folder and Browse… start in the project you have open, or in your home folder when none is, instead of wherever the system dialog was last (often Downloads).

Diagrams: a code map of the imports between your folders (TypeScript and JavaScript, tsconfig paths included) and a database diagram of the tables and foreign keys in Prisma schemas and SQL migrations. Parsed on your machine; open it from the Explorer header or the command palette, double-click a box to open it in your editor, and copy either one as Mermaid.
Recipes: a new section to see, build and share factory recipes. Open it from the Factory sidebar, the start screen or the command palette.

Recipe builder: name it, start from a template or an existing recipe, add agent, check and pull request stages, and save. No YAML to write; placeholders like {spec.out} are one click, and it tells you what's missing before you save.

Share recipes: copy one as text, export it to a file, and import from a paste, the clipboard or a file. The import shows what it adds first, keeps your own agents, and never adds the same recipe twice.
A recipe stage with just a prompt runs on your default agent.
New factory run: what to build comes right after the recipe; per-stage agents and the start point fold away until you need them.
The Factory sidebar lists your recipes, with a run button on each.
Start screen: a Software Factory card with New run and Recipes.
Overview: "need you" now counts factory runs waiting for your approval, and factory runs show their status and recipe.

Repeat: run the same mission pass after pass, each building on the last. Set how many passes, the minutes between them and an optional check command (Factory → Automations → Repeat, or Repeat… on a mission or agent task). Unattended passes run in print mode and end when the agent exits; interactive ones end when you click Accept pass. Every pass is committed in the loop's worktree, the next one gets the last report and a failed check's output, and the loop stops when a pass changes nothing or the check fails twice.
CLI: sldev new --repeat 5 --gap 30m --check "npm test" runs the same loop from the terminal; --print runs a single agent that exits when done; sldev accept and sldev loops.
CLI on Windows: install it with npm like on Linux and macOS. The background daemon, git and helper processes no longer flash console windows, and notifications are Windows toasts.

CLI: Ctrl-b w shows the repository's GitHub Actions runs (rerun failed jobs, open one in the browser), Ctrl-b e opens the pane's folder in your editor and Ctrl-b v its changed files side by side. sldev open, sldev workflows and sldev clean (finished panes and their worktrees, asked first) do the same from the command line.

New mission form: the agent and profile come first, other agents to compare are one-click chips, and the folder, branch and model fold into one Options line that says what will happen. The whole form fits without scrolling.
Mission cards say the next step: Answer when the agent waits for you, Review 3 files when it's done, Build from this after a research or plan mission.
Start screen: type what an agent should do and press Enter to open the New mission form with it. With a project open, the agent card comes first.
Settings has jump links to its sections.
Factory graphs shrink to fit the panel before they scroll, and stage cards no longer squash the agent name.
Fix: a multi-line prompt echoed in the terminal drew as a staircase. Long prompts now show their first lines; the whole brief is in the mission details.
Fix: the Overview counted a mission started a moment ago only after up to 30 seconds.

Fix: Codex missions and factory stages failed to start with Codex 0.16x, which dropped the --full-auto flag. Workspace-write mode now uses --sandbox workspace-write, which old and new versions accept.
Save for later: write a mission now and launch it when you're ready. Saved missions sit under "Saved for later" in the Agents tab and Mission Control, and you can edit them before launching.

Review changes opens in a tab of its own: side by side or unified, a file list with folders, Viewed to fold a file away, and the acceptance criteria on top. The sidebars step aside while you review (Settings → Editor).
Diff in your editor: with VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf or a JetBrains IDE, open a file's changes in the editor's own diff view from the review.
Focus mode (Ctrl+Alt+F, Cmd+Alt+F on a Mac) hides both sidebars, and split panes have a maximize button.
Factory runs open their stage terminals below the pipeline instead of beside it, so the graph keeps its width.
Fix: the usage dashboard showed an empty grey block next to its tiles.

Mission kinds: Build, Research, Investigate, Plan, Review, Map project and Freeform. Each frames your brief for the job; Research and Review run in the agent's read-only mode, and Freeform sends your prompt exactly as written. Your own kinds are Markdown templates in .sldev/missions.
Build from this: a finished Research or Plan mission becomes the brief of a Build mission or the start of a factory run.

Continue on another agent: when Claude Code, Codex or another agent stops at its plan's usage limit, the next agent in your order picks up the work in the same folder (Settings → Agents). Factory stages can do it on their own.
Software Factory: run your own spec, build and review skills as stages (skill: in a recipe), swap the agent or skill of any stage for one run, and start a run from a spec you already have.
Automations: start a recipe or a mission on a schedule, when CI fails on a branch, or when an issue gets a label. They run while the app is open and never push.

Project context: what agents learn goes into .sldev/memory.md and a local index linked to your code. Missions are pointed at the notes that match their brief, and the Context tab lets you browse, search and pin them.
Mission Control: missions, factory runs and usage in one tab, as status columns, a grid or a list.
Needs you for every agent: approval prompts on screen now count, not only the terminal bell, so OpenCode, Codex and Gemini dialogs show up. Mission details say how each agent's status is known.
Agents that don't report back get their final screen as the mission's report.
Fix: a Claude Code reply written just after it finished could be lost, leaving the report empty and Build from this disabled. Missions that lost it get it back on the next start.
Tab layout: keep open terminals as tabs on top, or list them down the left side of each group (Settings → Terminal → Tab layout, or "Toggle tab layout" in the command palette).
Fix: the resize cursor (↔) could stay stuck everywhere after dragging a sidebar edge if the window lost focus mid-drag.
Fix: GitHub Workflows showed "Unexpected end of JSON input" for a repository without Actions. It now says the repository has no workflows yet.
A right sidebar with Overview, Agents, Skills and Workflows tabs. Overview shows what needs you, today's usage and the latest missions. Hide it to a slim icon rail (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+B, ⌘⌥B on Mac).

Copy from terminals: right-click for Copy, Paste, Select all and Copy all output. Ctrl+C copies when text is selected, and Ctrl+V pastes on Windows. In agent screens, hold Shift while dragging to select (Option on Mac).
Fix: Cursor missions failed on Windows. Cursor now starts as "agent" (or "cursor-agent" on older installs), and prompts arrive whole.
Fix: on Windows, a task that runs a .ps1 script opened it in Notepad. It now runs in PowerShell.

Fix: the app could freeze for a while, mostly on Windows. Token usage is now read incrementally, and tool lookups no longer block the app. If it still happens, About → Copy diagnostics lists each freeze.
GitHub Workflows splits into Workflows and Runs sections that scroll on their own, and workflow logs open on Windows too.
New shell tasks offer the scripts in their folder (package.json, Makefile, justfile, …) to pick from.
What's new: after an update, sldev-io shows what changed (also under Help → What's new, and on the website's changelog).
Report a bug or send an idea from the app: it opens a GitHub issue with your versions already filled in.
The taskbar and dock icon shows how many missions need you.
Optional sound when a mission needs you (Settings → General).
Fix: on Windows, agents received only part of the prompt (sometimes a single word). Agents now start without a shell, and every prompt arrives whole, with its line breaks, quotes and symbols.
Removing a mission asks first, says what is removed and kept, and never throws away uncommitted work unless you tick it. The same goes for every other delete.
Missions take acceptance criteria, keep the agent's final report, and take your handoff notes. Follow-up and Second opinion pass both on to the next agent.
Agents dashboard: every running agent with what it's doing, how long it has run and its tokens. Ctrl+Shift+J jumps to the next one that needs you.
Software Factory: recipes run agents and checks as a pipeline, with bake-offs, PR feedback and run history.
Agent profiles, rules sync to every agent's instruction file, and a usage dashboard with a timeline and estimated cost.
Missions, factory runs, skills and tasks can work in any folder: type a path, Browse…, or pick a recent one.
A new look: one colour per status everywhere, counts on the sidebar icons, start cards in the empty dock, Ping and Save & Connect for SSH hosts.
The version is shown in the title bar; click it to open Settings → About.
The terminal installer always installs the version from the website, even over a local build.
Automatic updates on Windows and Linux; on macOS the app tells you when a new version is out.
Settings → About with versions, diagnostics to copy and links to the legal pages.
The Linux build runs on older distributions (glibc 2.35 and newer).
Installers are published to the public downloads page.
The free beta runs until the date on the website.
First beta: terminals, runtimes and tasks, agent missions for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Agent, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and custom CLIs.
Skills, workflows, notes, SSH with a credential vault, Docker containers and a first-run setup check.
